svg.title: Defence & vaccination
svg.desc: Skin & nose: Skin: physical barrier; antimicrobial substances and clotting at cuts help protect. Nose: hairs and mucus trap pathogens and particles. These barriers are non-specific: they act against many pathogens. Airways & stomach: Trachea/bronchi: mucus traps pathogens; cilia move mucus to the throat for swallowing. Stomach hydrochloric acid kills many swallowed pathogens. White blood cells: Phagocytosis: engulf and digest pathogens. Antibodies: bind specific pathogen antigens and help destroy the pathogen. Antitoxins: neutralise bacterial toxins. Different white cells have different roles. Specificity: An antibody’s binding site has a shape complementary to its antigen. Antibodies target antigens; antitoxins neutralise toxins. They are not interchangeable terms. Vaccination sequence: Dead/inactive pathogen or antigens → white cells make specific antibodies → memory cells remain. Later exposure → faster, larger antibody response, destroying pathogens before significant illness. Population protection: High vaccine uptake leaves fewer susceptible hosts, reducing transmission and helping protect those unable to be vaccinated. Evaluate disease reduction against reliable risk evidence, cost, access and uptake. Protection is not identical for every person.
